the_trap_that_made_this_non_trivial.what: reject.Reply(pkt) CANNOT be reused here. Reply's first act is `if !ok || Excluded(pkt) { return nil }`, and reject.Excluded returns true for every local destination (reject.isLocal: loopback, RFC1918, link-local, multicast, broadcast). So Reply returns nil for exactly the packets this task is about.
the_trap_that_made_this_non_trivial.fix: New exported reject.RST(pkt) — the same tcpRST builder Reply uses, with no Excluded question: TCP in, RST out, nil for anything else (not TCP, garbage, an RST itself — no loops). No policy inside; who deserves an answer is the caller's call. Still one RST builder in the product.
the_trap_that_made_this_non_trivial.why_the_two_lists_differ: Excluded answers 'what the §5.6 responder has no right to answer' — such a packet is not refused, it is simply none of our business. Verdict Bypass answers 'what to let out to the local network'. Where the bypass path refuses a flow, the second question is already settled and the first list would gag the answer.
the_trap_that_made_this_non_trivial.pinned_by: TestBypassTCPNeedsRSTBecauseReplyStaysSilent (internal/netstack) and TestRSTAnswersWhereReplyStaysSilent (internal/reject) — both assert BOTH halves (Reply is silent, RST answers), so a 'simplification' back to Reply reddens the explanation, not only T33.

decision_udp_stays_a_drop.answer: No. UDP refused by the bypass sink (ErrUnsupported / ErrDisabled / socket error) keeps its silent, counted Stats.Blocked drop. TestBypassSendErrorCountsAsBlocked keeps `Stats.Blocked == 1` unchanged — nothing about the UDP path moved.
arguments_strongest_first: RFC 1122 §3.2.2 forbids generating an ICMP error in response to a datagram addressed to a broadcast or multicast address — and mDNS (224.0.0.251), SSDP (239.255.255.250) and DHCP (255.255.255.255) are precisely what the bypass path exists for. The same instinct is already encoded in reject.isLocal, which puts multicast and broadcast among the exceptions.

ICMPv4PortUnreachable would be a lie about a third party: it says 'nobody is listening on that port there', while what actually failed is our own socket. A refusal that misstates the cause is worse than silence — it sends diagnosis the wrong way. The TCP RST, by contrast, tells the truth about our own path.

There is nothing to rescue from a timeout. §5.6 justifies 'refusal, not silence' by applications hanging until their timeout. TCP-to-LAN is literally that (connect hangs tens of seconds). Service discovery is the opposite: connectionless, periodic, retried by design, nobody waiting.

The UDP refusal is transient, the TCP one is permanent. ErrNoInterface / WriteTo failures pass in a second; answering ICMP turns a momentary unreadiness into a hard error at the client (net.UDPConn surfaces ICMP on a connected socket as a connection error). The bypass path's refusal of TCP never changes — it follows from the shape of the path, not the state of the network.

ErrDisabled specifically: the bypass_sink policy exists so that switching it off reproduces pre-policy behavior, i.e. the silent drop. Answering ICMP under it would break that contract and negcheck's meaning for it.

decision_own_flag.answer: Own flag, bypass_tcp_reject. reject_mode was NOT reused.
arguments: reject_mode's doc says fail-close ('fail-close через RST/ICMP, а не дроп (§5.6, T12, T13)'), and T33 runs on a stand with a LIVE node. The tunnel is open; the refusal means 'this path will not carry this flow', not 'there is no way out'. Merging them would either falsify that doc comment or widen it to 'all refusals go silent', after which T12/T13's 'падает без чего' column in §8.3 stops being accurate.

The precedent next door is exactly this shape: bypass_sink is also a bypass-path flag whose off-state is the silent drop, and it did not become part of reject_mode either. The dividing line the codebase already drew: reject_mode is about the phase (fail-close), bypass flags are about the path.
negcheck loses resolution on merge — reject_mode's guard set would become a union of two independent claims, and 'red without reject_mode' would stop naming one cause.
decision_own_flag.counter_argument_weighed_and_rejected: Two flags allow an incoherent combination (reject_mode=drop with bypass_tcp_reject on: hop silent in fail-close, talkative on LAN). It does not weigh: policies are not a user setting but a falsifiability stand, and they are disabled one at a time precisely so each reddens its own check.
decision_own_flag.registered: internal/policy/policies.go, next to BypassSink; guard TestT33TCPToLocalNetworkGetsRST, verified red under HOP_DISABLE=bypass_tcp_reject (no RST is built at all and the test waits out the full WaitTimeout). Guard test was written and seen red BEFORE the implementation, in a separate commit (aa12c42), the order both previous passes followed.

changed_files.what: New exported RST(pkt []byte) []byte — TCP RST with no Excluded check, nil for non-TCP/garbage/an RST. Reply is untouched and still gates on Excluded; both share tcpRST.

handle()'s case Bypass answers TCP with s.refuseBypassTCP(pkt) and returns, BEFORE ever calling Bypass.Send. New method refuseBypassTCP: under policy.BypassTCPReject it calls reject.RST, counts Stats.Rejected and writes through the single-writer s.write; nil answer or the policy off falls through to Stats.Blocked (silence must stay observable). The BypassSink interface doc now states the UDP-only contract explicitly, so an implementation need not learn to refuse by protocol.
New policy BypassTCPReject (bypass_tcp_reject), registered in All() next to BypassSink. Doc carries the short form of why it is not reject_mode.

ExpectRST and ExpectICMPUnreach now WAIT (up to WaitTimeout) via a shared expect() helper on the same Written() channel and the same clock.System{}.After that WaitEmitted uses. They used to look only at what was already written, which made them unusable as intended: Emitted() drains, so 'WaitEmitted then ExpectRST' handed back an empty queue, and 'ExpectRST straight away' raced the pump. Behavior for already-written packets is unchanged; the only previous caller (fake_test.go) writes synchronously and needed no edit.

new_tests.note: T33 is the registered guard for bypass_tcp_reject. It runs on a HEALTHY stand on purpose — that is what makes it not-fail-close and therefore not reject_mode's business. Positive half: RST on the device, addressed lanHost -> client. Negative half: h.byp.Packets() empty (nothing reached the bypass sink) and h.dialer.TCPDialed() empty (nothing was dialed into the tunnel), plus Stats.Rejected == 1 && Blocked == 0. It synchronizes on ExpectRST's own wait, never on fakenet.Bypass.WaitPackets, which waits forever and would hang instead of reddening. The seam test is the mirror of TestRejectVerdictNeverEndsInSilence: for five LAN destinations it asserts classify == Bypass, reject.Reply == nil, reject.RST != nil.
The same seam asserted from the reject side, plus RST's own contract: nil for its own output (no loop), for UDP, for garbage and for nil.

TestBypassSendErrorCountsAsBlocked (internal/netstack) — Stats.Blocked == 1 expectation deliberately NOT changed; the UDP refusal path is unchanged by design (see decision_udp_stays_a_drop).

deviations: packettest.ExpectRST / ExpectICMPUnreach changed from 'look at what is already there' to 'wait up to WaitTimeout'. Touching a neighbouring package inside this task — yes; the alternative was worse: a third test re-parsing TCP flags by hand instead of using the ready helper. Same clock and same channel as WaitEmitted, so realtimelint stays quiet.

The refusal is built per packet, not once per flow. The verdict is remembered (flowTable, §3.4) but the answer is not cached: a SYN retransmit arriving before the RST reaches the client produces a second RST. The Reject branch (T12) behaves the same way, and it is more correct than remembering 'already answered' — a client that missed the first answer must get the second.

A configuration bypass rule naming a TCP flow now gets an RST rather than reaching the local network. Not a regression in configurability but its honest boundary: the bypass path is a UDP NAT (§6.8) and configuration cannot gift it TCP. Before this pass such a rule dropped the packet silently — the same lie, only quieter.
spec_edits: SPEC.md §6.10: new paragraph 'Путь несёт только UDP, и TCP по нему получает отказ, а не дроп' — states the UDP-only contract, the RST for TCP, and the RFC 1122 reason UDP stays a drop.

next_task.name: Invalidate bypass sockets on interface change
next_task.why_first: It is the last known hole in the bypass path that is a hole rather than a deferred feature, and the previous pass wrote it up as such: 'дыра, а не решение'. §6.8's 'следствие первое' says outright that a socket's binding is immutable and a network change means the old sockets must be re-dialed. Nothing does that today, and the observable symptom is a growing Stats.Blocked with no explanation — or, worse, traffic leaving through the interface the user just left.
current_state: bypass.NAT binds every socket to whatever Selector.Interface() returned at its creation (internal/bypass/bypass.go, socketFor -> the Control func passed in Config) and never re-binds it. The NAT's lifetime is tied to a.stack (agent Up/Down), and switching Wi-Fi -> Ethernet tears down neither.

Worse: sock.seen is refreshed on every Send (internal/bypass/bypass.go, the socketFor path), not only on a successful round trip. A client that retries mDNS/SSDP every few seconds — and service discovery does exactly that — keeps a socket that is dead by binding alive forever: the Idle sweep (default 60 s) never sees it as idle. Not 'it will go away after 60 s of quiet' but 'it will never go away while the client keeps asking'.

Nothing ties the NAT's socket cache to outbound.Selector's interface-change signal. agent.NetworkChanged exists and is poked directly by tests; whether the event reaches it from the OS is checked by no level at all (docs/verification-agent.md says this about T6 and it holds for the wiring too).
Full writeup: implementation-notes.md, 'Этап 9 — BypassSink', Deviations, the paragraph 'Смена интерфейса не инвалидирует уже открытые bypass-сокеты — дыра, а не решение'.
next_task.goal: A bypass socket bound to an interface that is no longer the outbound interface stops being used: either it is closed on the interface-change signal and the next Send re-dials, or it dies of age regardless of traffic. Decide which — and argue it — rather than implementing both.
shapes: NAT.Reset() called by outbound.Selector's rtnetlink watcher on interface change: close all sockets, next Send re-dials. Precise, but wiring it properly touches the watcher, which is why the BypassSink pass called it out of scope (the previous HANDOFF cited 'Global Constraint 9, constraints.md' — note that constraints.md does not exist anywhere in this repo or worktree, so that citation cannot be checked; treat the scope argument on its merits).

A hard TTL on socket age, independent of seen, so a socket dies by age even under continuous traffic. Cheaper and entirely inside internal/bypass, but it is a timer, not a signal: it papers over the symptom (a wedged socket) instead of reacting to the cause (the interface changed).
The two are not exclusive — the TTL is a floor under the signal — but shipping both without saying which one is the mechanism would leave the next reader unable to tell which is load-bearing.
reuse: internal/agent already has NetworkChanged and already fans out events; the bypass NAT's lifetime already lives next to a.stack in Up/Down/watchService (internal/agent/wire.go).
bypass.NAT already has close() and a sweep on its own clock.Clock, so both shapes have somewhere to live.
internal/l3/bypass_test.go (T31) is the existing stand that drives a real physical interface in a netns; a second veth is the natural way to make an interface change real rather than mocked.

test_gap.stays_green: T31 (TestBypassMDNSReachesPhysicalInterfaceAndReturnsViaNAT, internal/l3), T17, T32, T33, TestBypassSendErrorCountsAsBlocked, and the internal/bypass suite.
test_gap.missing_and_needed: A test where the interface changes under a live bypass socket and the next Send does NOT go out the old binding. Per-task gate only needs the new policy's own guard under HOP_DISABLE=<name>; the controller runs the full one at the end of the pass.
notes.realtimelint: does not accept ./... as an argument — pass literally `.`
notes.l3_how_to_run: Build once, run under an unprivileged user namespace: `go test -c -o /tmp/l3.test ./internal/l3` then `HOP_L3=1 unshare -Urn /tmp/l3.test` (add `-test.v -test.run '<pattern>'` to scope it). This works without root — unshare -Urn grants CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the fresh netns. Building the test binary once and reusing it across repeated unshare invocations is much faster than `go test` per run when iterating.

queue_after_bypass_tcp_reject.detail: bypass.NAT.Stats() is unreachable in production today — nothing outside internal/bypass/bypass_test.go calls it, and Stack.Stats() (internal/netstack/netstack.go) does not fold it in the way it folds in natTable's stats. In production the idle sweep of bypass sockets therefore only runs on Send, and persists until Down after traffic stops — parity with natTable, not a regression, but Stats() staying unreachable means bypass socket/goroutine counts are invisible to whatever eventually surfaces Stack.Stats (CLI status, metrics).
queue_after_bypass_tcp_reject.note: the BypassSink pass's final review (finding 9) fixed only the Stats() doc comment to say this plainly; wiring it into Stack.Stats is this queue item.
